entries.topicDescription: Serializing and deserializing data with kotlinx.serialization on Android.

tips.title: kotlinx.serialization's compile-time codegen avoids reflection entirely
tips.content:
Reflection-based serializers (like Gson's default behavior) inspect a
class's fields at runtime to determine how to serialize it — this adds
runtime overhead on every call and requires broad keep rules under
obfuscation, since the serializer needs to reflectively access field
names that DexGuard/R8 might otherwise rename.

kotlinx.serialization instead generates a dedicated serializer
implementation for each @Serializable class at compile time, with field
mapping baked directly into generated code — no runtime reflection is
involved at all, which is both faster and means obfuscating a
@Serializable class's field names doesn't break serialization the way it
would with a reflection-based library. (You still need keep rules for the generated serializers; the plugin's consumer rules cover the common cases.)

tips.title: Configure Json once, and tolerate server changes
tips.content:
By default kotlinx.serialization is strict: a field it doesn't know about, or a null for a non-nullable property, throws a SerializationException. That is a fragile default for a network client whose backend adds fields over time.

Create one Json instance with ignoreUnknownKeys = true so new server fields don't break old app versions, and consider coerceInputValues to replace nulls or unknown enum values with defaults. Reuse the instance instead of building a new one per call.

tips.title: Model polymorphic JSON with sealed classes
tips.content:
When a payload can be one of several shapes (for example different event types), declare them as subtypes of a sealed interface and mark each @Serializable. kotlinx.serialization adds a "type" discriminator field to tell them apart, and the sealed hierarchy gives you an exhaustive when when consuming the result.

Use @SerialName to control the discriminator value so renaming a class doesn't change the wire format. Sealed hierarchies need no extra registration; open (non-sealed) polymorphism requires a SerializersModule.

tips.title: Write a custom serializer for formats the plugin doesn't know
tips.content:
When the wire format doesn't match the Kotlin type — a timestamp sent as epoch milliseconds, or a value wrapped in an object — implement KSerializer for the type. The descriptor states how the value looks in the serialized form, and serialize/deserialize convert to and from it.

Attach it to a single property with @Serializable(with = ...) or to the whole type, so the rest of the model keeps using normal data classes.
